title: Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children
content:
(Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch said today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

Humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

title: What the EU can learn from Mark Carney on digital sovereignty
content:
At Davos earlier this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered a compelling response to a world increasingly shaped by great-power rivalry. Middle powers need greater strategic autonomy, he argued, but they cannot secure it by retreating behind their borders.

Instead, they need to build their own capabilities while working more closely with like-minded partners. On technology, he reasoned that countries should cooperate so they are not ultimately forced to choose between “hegemons and hyperscalers.”

At the recent EU-Canada Summit, that philosophy began to translate into policy. Canada and the EU launched an “Alliance for the Future” based on closer economic, technological and strategic cooperation. They also concluded negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement designed to support a “secure, open and trusted digital environment”​ resilient economic relations​,​ and trusted cross-border data flows.

That principle matters not only for Europe’s new relationship with Canada, but for its approach to other trusted partners.

Sovereignty without isolation

title: Saudi Arabia/UN: Closure of ILO complaint a blow for migrant workers facing persistent abuse and discrimination
content:
Responding to the closure of the labour rights complaint filed against Saudi Arabia under Article 26 of the International Labour Organization (ILO) Constitution, following an agreement reached between Saudi Arabia and workers’ representative to the ILO, Iain Byrne, Amnesty International’s Head of Economic and Social Justice, said: 

“The premature closure of the formal complaint at the ILO against Saudi Arabia is a blow for the millions of migrant workers in the country.  

“The concerns that gave rise to the complaint remain unresolved. They include serious abuses linked to the persistence of the kafala system, which continues to leave migrant workers dependent on their employers and enables forced labour, exploitation and racial discrimination, while imposing substantial barriers to accessing justice.  

“While the agreement reached between the trade unions and the government sets out broad areas for future engagement, it fails to detail any specific legal or policy changes that Saudi Arabia has committed to undertake. It also fails so far to provide clear timelines for action, publicly available benchmarks or an independent monitoring mechanism.

title: In Brazil’s elections, big techs’ transparency and cooperation policies translate as governance washing, according to this expert
content:
Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University NetLab has been following closely how this election unfolds on social media

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Art by Global Voices, created in Canva Pro.

Amid a series of corruption scandals, the 2026 general election in Brazil is also flooded with headlines about social media companies’ role in the campaign. Users supporting the candidacy of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent center-left candidate running for re-election, have been reporting a sudden drop in their Instagram Stories views when posting about politics. They say that Meta AI refused to generate images featuring Lula’s name and party number, while delivering the same request for Flávio Bolsonaro, his far-right opponent and the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro.

On October 16, Meta admitted technical problems on its platforms which affected how pro-Lula content was delivered to users. As reported by the Associated Press, despite acknowledging “global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures, and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression,” the company that owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook denied any political bias.

    Told through the eyes of Margarita herself, the film offers a rare portrait of an ancient way of life from a fresh, surprising voice – not an elder or chief, but a young woman standing at a crossroads, questioning her future.

    Margarita’s coming-of-age story unfolds in the present while gaining depth and resonance through intimate family footage spanning over 20 years. With her voice always at the center, she guides us through a tapestry of past and present, revealing a story of extraordinary change in the High Arctic.

title: The Nvidia Scandal Exposes American Blind Spots
content:
Washington has built an elaborate web of export controls and licensing requirements to keep artificial intelligence chips from reaching China.

Yet Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s apparent “honeytrap” affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of passing information to Beijing, is about more than the blind spots of those controls. It is about the difficulty of shutting down access to advanced tech in a globalized, interconnected world — and about a company, a regulator, and an executive branch that saw warning signs and were slow act on them. 

Had existing rules been enforced, Nvidia should never have been selling advanced chips to the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International. Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, which became a major Nvidia customer, and attracted scrutiny over possible violations of American export controls. Nvidia’s board has retained outside counsel to investigate whether Chinese intelligence targeted their former CEO, who resigned after his affairs were revealed. The company maintains that it has no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised.
snippet: Washington has built an elaborate web of export controls and licensing requirements to keep artificial intelligence chips from reaching China.

title: Advancing CC Signals: Preparing for Public Alpha Testing in 2027
content:
How can we give the people and organizations that share and make collections of knowledge and creativity available in the commons a meaningful way to encourage reciprocity from AI developers?

This question is central to Creative Commons’ ongoing development of CC Signals, a framework of legal tools and guiding norms designed to encourage reciprocity in how AI systems use shared knowledge. 

On November 2-3, Creative Commons convened a group of open knowledge organizations in Chicago to advance this work. Building on earlier conversations and workshops with legal, policy, and technical experts, the two-day gathering focused on refining the first CC Signals legal tool and preparing for the release of an alpha version in early 2027. 

The gathering brought together several organizations exploring early adoption of CC Signals, bringing perspectives from open journalism, scholarly publishing, education, and cultural heritage. Participants included representatives from the Wikimedia Foundation, The Conversation, Cambridge University Press and Assessment, MIT Open Learning, Munch Museum, and Civic News Company.
snippet: How can we give the people and organizations that share and make collections of knowledge and creativity available in the commons a meaningful way to encourage reciprocity from AI developers?

title: Commission hosts Apply AI Summit to boost Europe’s AI innovation and uptake
content:
Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels tomorrow.

They will discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects. 

Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will host the summit and present the first Apply AI Startup Award to three European start-ups. title: “If Europe doesn’t get its act together, we’re all screwed” – Toomas Hendrik Ilves
content:
Karolina Zbytniewska: Do you think a new global order is emerging? And where does Europe fit into it?

I think Europe needs to figure out what it must do to remain alive. Europe has fallen dramatically behind in technology, and that is an existential problem. We have seen an unelected billionaire being able to switch off satellite communications to Ukraine. We are dependent on Starlink and Starshield, while our own low-Earth-orbit satellite capabilities are only beginning to develop.

We are also far behind in artificial intelligence. American private-sector investment in AI was around $400 billion last year and is approaching $700 billion this year, while Europe is investing a fraction of that.

Unless we get our act together, the European Union may not break up, but it will move towards a multi-speed Europe.

title: Searching for a good day for honey
content: On a perfect summer's day in Latvia, there’s barely any wind and the flowers are producing nectar. “20 degrees and up, with sunshine – that’s an ideal day,” says Valters Brusbārdis, who kept bees for 30 years before selling them all last spring. He also chairs the Latvian Beekeepers’ Association. June and July are usually the most reliable months for making honey, he said. For a professional beekeeper in Latvia, more than 50kg of honey per colony makes a good season. Some of his fellow beekeepers told him they’d had record harvests this year. In 2023, Eurostat counted a record 9.4 million hives on EU farms, 16% more than in 2020. Italy had the highest number, followed by Romania, and Greece. But the figures exclude wild bees, and tell us nothing about the health of the bees living in these hives. Bees and the climate In Bulgaria’s Pirin Mountains, beekeeper Ivan Geshev has seen the effects of the climate crisis on his bees since 2016, from droughts to sharp temperature swings. He estimates that his summer worker bees now live five or six days less than they used to, leaving fewer bees to collect pollen and nectar. Spring is particularly tricky, just as bee colonies begin to grow

content:

What should Interreg Baltic Sea Region, as a transnational cooperation programme, address after 2027? As work on the future Programme progresses, dialogue with regional stakeholders help further develop the cooperation needs identified by the Programme countries. title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
content:
When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.

The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. 

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: 

Its own leaders. 

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.

Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.

title: FPF sues Defense Department for info on media ‘blacklist’
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Nov. 16, 2026 — The Department of Defense is unlawfully withholding information about a media “blacklist” it has admitted to keeping internally, according to a lawsuit filed today in federal court by Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) and The Intercept.

The plaintiffs, represented by Free Information Group, are asking the court to force the department to disclose documents related to a list of journalists it “disregards,” as described by DOD personnel.

In July, Intercept reporter Nick Turse posed several questions to U.S. Central Command about Iranian attacks on U.S. bases across the Middle East. He was told by CENTCOM staff that if his inquiries on the topic did not stop, he would be put on an existing, internal “list of people to disregard.” A U.S. official later told Turse that the DOD “had a standing order not to engage with” him.

CENTCOM has ignored Freedom of Information Act requests from both Turse and Lauren Harper, FPF’s Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, for copies of the list of journalists CENTCOM “disregards.”

title: Civil society questions decree that could block access to telecommunications networks in Mozambique
content:
Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression

Originally published on Global Voices

Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025. Photo by Wilson Thole. Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension. The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

title: OPINION: African Democracy on Life Support
content:
By The Rev. Gabriel Odima*

MINNESOTA, USA | 16 November 2026 (IDN) — Africa has become a household name across North America, Europe, Australia, South America and Asia. The only images beaming on the world’s television screens are hunger-stricken skeletons, civil wars, political abductions, human rights abuses and a move towards single-party or no-party rule in countries like Uganda, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Niger, Benin, Tanzania, Gabon and Sudan, to name a few. Democracy is on life support across Africa, and this is a troubling trend.

In the case of Uganda, the military regime, from its installation in 1986 by the gun and bloodshed, has consistently, arrogantly and cynically suppressed and never permitted citizens and their organised political parties to enjoy the freedom to hold opinions on political or public matters, except the opinions of the regime.

In August 1992, the military rulers in Uganda decided to discard their cloak of disguise, which had enabled them since 1986 to falsely present their regime as a coalition in which political parties were represented.

title: Natnael Getenew Zeleke oppi koodaamaan 14-vuotiaana lukemalla setänsä paperista kirjaa – Sitten hän keksi, miten tekoälyä voi hyödyntää ilman nettiä
content:
Pitkä lento ei tunnu vaivaavan Natnael Getenew Zelekeä pätkääkään. Hän on pirteä ja intoa täynnä marraskuisessa Helsingissä, kun hän ensimmäistä kertaa saapuu Eurooppaan.

Helsingistä matka jatkuu Turkuun. Siellä hän osallistuu hackathoniin, eli kilpailuun, jossa keksitään uusia ohjelmistoja ja teknisiä ratkaisuja. 

Sellaisia hän on voittanut jo useita, vaikka onkin vasta 25-vuotias. Suurin saavutus tähän mennessä on Amazonin järjestämän AWS Innovation Awardin voittaminen. Kilpailuun osallistui noin 10 000 kehittäjätiimiä 115 maasta, ja palkintorahoja koko kilpailussa jaettiin 250 000 euroa.  

Voittanut sovellus on nimeltään Ivy. Se on tekoälypohjainen oppimisratkaisu, joka toimii myös ilman internetyhteyttä.  

 Getenew Zeleke tiesi jo teininä, että palkkatyö ei ole häntä varten. Hän halusi olla oma pomonsa omassa yrityksessään. Se oli vanhemmille hieman hankala asia sulatettavaksi.  

“Etiopiassa ajatellaan edelleen vahvasti, että opiskelu ja tutkinto ovat ainoa oikea tie menestykseen”, hän sanoo.

title: 8th International Open Search Symposium – A review (day one)
content:
On the morning of 7 October, the conference kicked off at CODE University of Applied Sciences in Berlin.
First on the mic were Peter Ruppel, President of CODE University of Applied Sciences and Fabian Geier, Professor of Philosophy at CODE University who both welcomed the participants with dedicated kick-off addresses.

“Sovereignty has become a political buzzword. This community can give it substance and it can share how it can look in practice, how to comply, how it can be governed and how it can earn trust from users.” said Peter Ruppel in his welcome address.

„It is pretty clear we are a bit cornered in Europe. In an era where bullying becomes the norm, it is unwise to not be in charge of the technology that we run our societies on.“ stated Fabian Geier.

“This is a conference for Europeans who are builders! (…) I am thankful that OSF is here and to all the people doing the work to help us become a bit more independent as Europeans and not just be on the receiving end of power but built autonomy through technology!” he added, expressing hope for hands-on solutions being shaped in Europe and underlining the importance of conferences like #ossym.

title: Mitä toiseuttaminen tekee kuulumisen kokemukselle?
content:
Yhteiskunnan toistuvalla riskipuheella on erilaisia vaikutuksia lapsiin ja nuoriin. Jokaisella on oikeus tulla nähdyksi yhteiskunnan täysivaltaisena jäsenenä.

Yhteiskunnallinen keskustelu lapsista ja nuorista on ollut syksyn 2026 aikana eri tavoin jännitteistä. Siinä toki ei ole mitään uutta, että lapsista ja nuorista puhutaan riskien, uhkien ja kontrollin näkökulmasta, mutta millä tavoin lapsia ja nuoria koskevassa yhteiskunnallisessa keskustelussa rakennetaan ulkopuolisuutta?

Aikuiset ovat hanakoita määrittämään lasten ja nuorten paikan, jolloin lasten ja nuorten oma toimijuus jää kapeaksi, eikä pääsyä mukaan julkiseen keskusteluun välttämättä ole.  Olennainen kysymys onkin, otetaanko lapset ja nuoret mukaan keskusteluun vai puhutaanko heidän ohitseen.

Lasten ympärillä käydään paljon keskustelua lasten parhaasta, mutta huomattavasti harvemmin siitä, miten erilaiset puhetavat muokkaavat lasten mahdollisuuksia tulla nähdyiksi yhteisön täysivaltaisina jäseninä.

Lapset näyttäytyvät keskusteluissa helposti joko vaaralle alttiina tai vaaran aiheuttajina. Lapsia suojellaan ja heitä kontrolloidaan, usein samanaikaisesti.

title: Beyond DMT: why the true power of Brazil’s sacred jurema plant is social, not just psychedelic
content:
Jurema-preta is the name of both a plant – Mimosa tenuiflora – and an indigenous spiritual tradition of northeastern Brazil. The plant is used to make a potentially hallucinogenic brew that is consumed in sacred rituals. The exact mixture of herbs and other elements contained in the brew is a secret known only by jurema mestre shamans and never revealed.

In 2024 I had the opportunity to visit, as an anthropologist, the city of Natal, in Brazil’s Rio Grande do Norte region, which is a hotspot of the jurema cult. While there, I learned that jurema’s power is as much social as it is chemical.

The sacred and molecular properties of the plant are currently fostering all manner of exciting (though challenging) connections between indigenous knowledge and neuroscience. But jurema’s power goes beyond the plant and its ceremonies, as the jurema cult provides a radically plural space that welcomes all kinds of non-normative identities.

title: Why marine climate refugia matters for safeguarding the world’s oceans
content:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Marine climate refugia are areas where relatively stable environmental conditions help species and ecosystems withstand climate change.

  • They are identified through three approaches: low exposure, ecological resilience and habitat suitability.

    The ocean is changing rapidly. Warming, acidification, oxygen loss, sea-level rise, and the intensification of extreme events are transforming marine ecosystems, leading to species shifts and mass mortality events. However, these impacts are not distributed evenly. There are areas that buffer these effects and act as true “marine climate refugia”.

title: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
content:
On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.

The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.

Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.

By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.

title: Chinamaxxing on geopoliittista trollausta parhaimmillaan
content:
Uudenlaisen Kiina-meemeilyn tulkitseminen Kiinan pehmeän vallan kasvuksi ei riitä. Kyse on myös siitä, että osa länsimaalaisista nuorista kieltäytyy tulkitsemasta Kiinaa ylhäältä annetuista raameista.

Absurdin huumorin ystävät ovat saaneet maistiaisia kiinankielisestä sisällöstä jo muita pidempään. Meemiveteraanit muistavat, kun jo vuonna 2020 laulettiin ”xue hua piao piaota” ja vuonna 2021 yhdysvaltalainen näyttelijä John Cena söi jäätelöä ja puhui kiinaa… innokkaasti. Bing chilling!

Ja nyt meillä on chinamaxxing.

Vuonna 2025 nousseella chinamaxxingilla tarkoitetaan yleensä Kiinaan liittyvää somesisältöä, jossa henkilö kokee tulleensa kiinalaiseksi. Meemeissä kiinalaisuutta ovat esimerkiksi vakuutteleminen kuuman veden juomisen terveellisyydestä, ketjupolttaminen tai Tsingtao-oluen juominen. Jotkut vaikuttajat ovat puolestaan tehneet samantyylisiä jumppaliikkeitä kuin kiinalaiset tädit ja sedät puistoissa. Sävy on myönteinen ja hassutteleva. 

Yhteiskunnallisinta on taas sisältö, jossa ihaillaan Kiinan infrastruktuuria, luotijunaverkostoa tai Chongqingin kaltaisten vauraiden suurkaupunkien futuristista ulkonäköä. Sanotaan, että Kiina elää tulevaisuudessa.

content:

Venäjä käyttää kryptovaroja yhä enemmän rajat ylittäviin maksuihin ja hankintoihin kiertäen perinteisiä pankkikanavia ja maksuliikennejärjestelmiä. Ne mahdollistavat Venäjälle pääsyn tavaroihin ja teknologioihin, joita se käyttää hyökkäyssodassaan Ukrainaa vastaan.

Suomi, Tanska, Viro, Ranska ja Liettua vaativat tulevissa pakoteneuvotteluissa vahvempia toimia Venäjän käyttämiin kryptovaroihin ja niihin liittyviin toimijoihin puuttumiseksi.

title: Europe: Disgraceful Rwanda deportation deal repeats mistakes of the past
content:
Reacting to today’s announcement from the Vienna Migration Conference where Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans to carry out deportations to so-called “return hubs” in Rwanda, Aimée Stuflesser, the asylum and migration expert at Amnesty International Austria, said:

“Today’s disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past. Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights.

“Undocumented people must not become pawns in a politics of deterrence. The harms of these types of migration deals are well documented. From the Italy–Albania deal and the UK’s attempt to forcibly send people to Rwanda, to Australia’s offshore detention system, past attempts to send people to countries to which they have no connection have proven unlawful, unworkable and expensive.

title: "Coffers Are Never Empty…For Bombs": Climate Activist Asad Rehman on Need for Climate Finance
content:
The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need.

“Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, 'Our coffers are empty.' But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

title: Navigating the tricky borders of AI scribes in healthcare
content:
The potential of AI has definitely not been lost on the healthcare sector. AI has the ability to solve many long-standing problems in modern healthcare: lack of resources, risks of human error and difficulties in serving a rapidly evolving patient base. While risks and concerns exist, the AI transformation of the patient journey and other healthcare processes seems inevitable, both in the private and public sectors.

AI scribes, namely AI tools with the ability to convert human interactions into transcripts, visit summaries and other clinical documentation, appear to be a key example of this development. The typical use case is that an appointment between a patient and medical professional is recorded by an AI tool, converted into text and arranged into legally required medical record entries. As a result, the doctor can focus fully on the patient interaction without having to take meticulous notes and save time afterwards as the AI tool has already drafted the required entries.

Legally, things get interesting when we look at what the AI scribe actually does and the extent to which the medical record entries and subsequent clinical activities rely on the AI scribe’s output.

title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
content:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.

Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.

title: Preserving memory through intergenerational collaboration in Lisbon
content:
Lisbon welcomed 19 participants during a European Heritage Hub Peer-Learning Visit from 4-6 November, exploring how community memories, oral histories and cultural heritage initiatives can strengthen social cohesion, foster intergenerational exchange and reinforce people’s sense of belonging.

Hosted by the City of Lisbon and organised in collaboration with Hub partner Eurocities, the visit focused on the municipal Memories of Lisbon Programme (Programa Memórias de Lisboa), selected as one of the Hub’s 10 Local Good Practices. The programme was led by Memory and Intangible Cultural Heritage Unit representatives Alexandra Aníbal and Mafalda Seoane.

The Memories of Lisbon Programme initiative connects a local older generation of storytellers with young people who interview, film and edit their testimonies about life in Lisbon — demonstrating how personal stories and local heritage can become powerful tools for community engagement, inclusion and cultural participation.

title: EU: Countries Plan Rwanda Deportation Centers
content:
(Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.

After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their plan to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

“History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”

title: The Students Beat the Strongman. Now What? Five Questions on What Comes Next For Serbia
content:
A new political party organized by student protesters made history last month when it ousted Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić at the polls, ending his party’s 14-year stranglehold on power. 

Long seen as immovable, Vučić was defeated by students who managed to rally support from across the country around a central, unifying goal: freeing Serbia’s institutions and economy from the corruption that flourished under the rule of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). 

Their electoral victory was decisive and undeniable. But dismantling the former regime’s networks of influence will not be easy. Serbia’s democratic credentials deteriorated under Vučić, with the leader and his party accused of cultivating extensive patronage networks inside the country’s judiciary, security forces, media, and private sector. 

The students, whose leaderless protest movement selected a range of political novices to represent them in parliament under the banner of the “Student List,” have vowed to restore independence to state bodies and end impunity for the corrupt.

title: Iraq Cracks Down on Oil Smuggling in Area Controlled by Iran-aligned Shiite Militias
content:
In a rare bid to assert state authority inside a paramilitary-controlled enclave, the Iraqi government has launched a campaign to dismantle oil smuggling networks in Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of Iran-backed militias along the Euphrates River, roughly 30 miles southwest of the capital.

The crackdown takes direct aim at an illicit fuel trade operating inside an area that has long functioned outside of Baghdad’s authority.

The move followed the leak of an intelligence report, seen by OCCRP, that detailed the smuggling operation and included satellite imagery showing container truck movements between pipelines and local storage facilities from 2022 to 2026. The report cited evidence of perforated oil pipelines and makeshift storage facilities, adding that the armed groups controlling the area smuggled the fuel along three suspected routes leading into Baghdad province.

title: Behold the Gloriously Cheap 1970s Italian Knockoffs Inspired by Star Wars
content:
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars,” pronounces the announcer in a TV news clip included in the new Nerdwriter video above. “It’s old-fashioned escapist entertainment, pure and simple.” That may have been all the Italian film industry needed to hear. The “spaghetti westerns” of the previous dozen years had proven that it could profitably master an American genre; surely it could do the same with a similar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fistful of Dollars, or even a Navajo Joe. Nerdwriter creator Evan Puschak goes over various instances of shameless imitation that characterize the Italian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

title: Google says Russian speakers pulled off first-ever fully automated AI cyberattack
content:
Russian-speaking hackers built an AI agent that carried out what may be the first-ever fully-automated cyberattack, Google reported Monday.

The tech giant’s cyber threat intelligence division said it had spotted hackers using artificial intelligence to “fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.”

The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks, which has dominated headlines and worried policymakers since AI firm Anthropic released its specialized model Mythos in April. 

Hackers, who used Russian in technical documentation identified by Google, set up a series of AI agents to “continuously compare pre- and post-patch code, identify vulnerabilities, and automatically develop exploits without human intervention,” Google said.

That means the agents independently found software flaws and ways to use them. The attackers targeted French websites in the media, entertainment and education sectors, Google said.

title: Measuring the value of public investment in open source for the European tech industry
content:
Open source powers Europe’s digital economy. A new report by the Sovereign Tech Agency and iconomy quantifies how public investment into open source strengthens European SMEs, the innovation economy and investors around them.

Europe’s digital economy runs on open source. Openly licensed software components and libraries are embedded throughout the products and services European companies rely on every day. Of the commercial codebases audited in 2026, 98% contained open source code. It is critical to the resilience, security, and competitiveness of the digital economy, but the work it takes to keep it running safely is often invisible, even to the businesses depending on it.

title: Tutkimus: Robotin välttelevä katse voi aiheuttaa ulkopuolisuuden tunnetta
content:
Johanna Kohvakka

Ihmiset suhtautuvat humanoidirobotteihin usein kuin tietoisiin toimijoihin ja tulkitsevat niiden eleitä sosiaalisina viesteinä. Katsekontaktia välttelevä robotti herätti voimakkaampia kielteisiä tunnereaktioita tutkimuksessa, joka tehtiin Tampereen yliopiston Human Information Processing -laboratoriossa.

"Ihmiset tapaavat suhtautua humanoidirobottien katse-eleisiin sosiaalisina viesteinä. Halusimme selvittää, mitä seuraa, kun robotti osoittaa välinpitämättömyyttä välttämällä katsekontaktia", tutkijatohtori Samuli Linnunsalo kertoo Tampereen yliopiston tiedotteessa.

Tutkimukseen osallistuneet olivat lyhyessä vuorovaikutustilanteessa humanoidirobotti NAOn kanssa. Robotti joko katsoi osallistujaa kohti tai vältti katsekontaktia. Tämän jälkeen osallistujat arvioivat kyselyissä ulkopuolisuuden tunnettaan, mielialaansa sekä neljän perustarpeen täyttymistä. Näitä olivat yhteenkuuluvuus, itsetunto, vuorovaikutustilanteen hallinta ja oman olemassaolon merkityksellisyys.

title: Survival in Ukraine’s Fortress Cities
content:
Driving around Kramatorsk, Sarah Ashton, Senior Sergeant of the 46th Brigade, points out what has been recently destroyed, what was hit months ago, and which businesses are still open. She also has a growing list of places she no longer wants to go.

Damaged bridges, demolished buildings, burned cars and stores whose names now serve as reference points for attacks accompany her journeys. Stopping for something to eat means leaving the vehicle outside and hoping it will still be intact when she returns.

An American serving in Ukrainian military intelligence, Sarah drives me through fortress-belt cities of Kramatorsk and neighboring Sloviansk. The cities are key to Vladimir Putin’s aim of capturing the Donbas, which comprises the oblasts of Luhansk and Donetsk in eastern Ukraine. He has now asked US mediators to persuade Kyiv to surrender this land, and it’s fair to describe this as No. 1 on the Kremlin’s list of demands.

A sliver of Luhansk and some 25% of Donetsk is still in government hands, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, two of its biggest cities. They used to each have a population of a couple of hundred thousand. Not anymore.

title: The antidote to TikTok tourism? A free paper map
content: Planning a city trip in Europe? Chances are you’ll scroll TikTok for ideas or ask ChatGPT to build an itinerary. But have you considered using a paper map instead? Sound old-school? It might be what you actually need. Meet USE-IT Europe, a network of free city maps made by young locals who want to share with visitors where they actually spend their time. The maps cover the usual ground – where to eat, drink, shop, relax – but each one also comes with a five-minute history of the city and an “Act like a local” section full of dos and don’ts. In Prague for example, don’t order the chimney cake. It’s “not Czech, not traditional, and not so good.” Depending on the city, you might also find Spotify playlists, useful local phrases, and suggestions on what to order at a bar or bring to a picnic in the park. The maps are full of practical tips too, from free concerts to places where you can get free tap water. “Honest tourist information from locals for young travellers. And nobody can pay to be on the map. title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
content:
When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top. 

Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children. 

Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. 

No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.

New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.

Ulkomaankauppa- ja kehitysministeri Ville Tavio (ps.) eväsi rahoituksen neljältä järjestöjen kehitysyhteistyöhankkeelta Somaliassa, joille virkahenkilöt olivat esittäneet rahoituksen myöntämistä.

Ulkoministeriön kehityspoliittisen osaston päällikkö Juha Savolainen linjasi Ilta-Sanomille pitävänsä ministeri Tavion päätöstä lainvastaisena. Savolaisen mukaan ministeri ei kohdellut neljää Somalia-hanketta hallintolain edellyttämällä tavalla tasapuolisesti.

title: Making injustice legal: How Israeli law legitimizes apartheid, genocide and impunity
content:
Israel’s laws are built to entrench ethnic domination, and international courts are under attack for noticing

Originally published on Global Voices

Roadblocks at the entrance to Shuhada Street in Hebron, Palestine. Photo by Travel 2 Palestine on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank are subject to Israeli civil law. Palestinians who suffer their violence and occupation are subject to Israeli military law. The two face two different legal systems. 

Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.

For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

title: Wealthy countries aren’t protected from climate extremes – Europe must adapt quickly too
content:
Extreme heatwaves across Europe led to significant annual deaths this summer. In Spain, floods in Valencia during 2024 killed 200 people and paralysed infrastructure. Germany’s 2021 floods highlighted severe weaknesses in early-warning communication, while wildfires in France led to large-scale evacuations and reduced air quality.

It’s easy to assume that strong institutions and technological capacity protect wealthy countries from the consequences of climate change. But evidence suggests otherwise. Well-resourced cities remain vulnerable to rapid-onset extremes. Our research across high-income countries identifies a fundamental challenge here: adaptation responsibility is frequently fragmented across governance levels.

The knock-on effects of climate-induced extremes also expose longstanding inequalities between people of different ages, genders and race, for example. Migrant, elderly and low-income communities are disproportionately affected by climate consequences. This is not simply because these communities are more exposed to the effects of extreme weather. Their vulnerabilities are also shaped by housing quality, income, health and lower political influence.

title: Global Warming Approaches 1.5 Degrees in "Calamity for the World's Ecosystems"
content:
As delegates, industry lobbyists and civil society activists attend this year’s United Nations climate summit, known as COP31, we speak with international environmental lawyer Farhana Yamin about the state of global climate efforts. Yamin helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement and has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits. The Paris Agreement aimed to keep global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a threshold that climate scientists say the world will now overshoot.

“It’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier,” says Yamin. “So, we’re about 10 years behind, but I hope that over time that we can accelerate.”

title: Donate Equity to Support Digital Rights: Stocks, DAFs, and Giving
content:
Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit?  

For 35 years, the Electronic Frontier Foundation has been advancing our digital rights, including defending security researchers, encrypting the web, and fighting illegal surveillance. Donating equity to EFF can help support this important work. 

Perhaps your family has taken advantage of the new tax law around giving by creating a Donor-Advised Fund.  

Perhaps your employer has gone public and you now own stock.  

Perhaps you’ve seen some of EFF’s recent successes and thought, Man, imagine what they could do with more. 

A gift of equity can help your contribution go farther and offer tax savings. When you donate appreciated stock, you avoid paying capital gains tax on any increase in its value. You also receive a charitable income tax deduction for the fair market value of appreciated stock on the date it is transferred. Also, more and more companies are offering gift-matching programs that can double your impact at no additional cost.

title: Sähkön hinta voi moninkertaistua hetkessä – maksuton Virtanen-palvelu kertoo, mihin sähkö todella kuluu
content:
Talvi lähestyy, ja sähkön hinnan voimakas vaihtelu tekee kulutuksen ajoittamisesta taas ajankohtaista. Vuonna 2026 pörssisähkön kuukausikeskihinta on vaihdellut rajusti: heinäkuun 1,93 sentistä helmikuun 17,22 senttiin kilowattitunnilta. Vuorokauden sisäinen vaihtelu on vielä suurempaa. Marraskuun 2026 alussa päivän halvimman ja kalleimman vartin hinnan ero oli melkein satakertainen.

Nitorin data-analyytikkojen kehittämä kaikille avoin, maksuton Virtanen.ai-työkalu auttaa kotitalouksia ymmärtämään, mihin sähköä todella kuluu. Uutuutena palvelussa voi nyt verrata pörssisähkön ja kiinteähintaisen sopimuksen eroja. Virtasella voi myös selvittää, onko noin vuosi sitten käyttöön otettu varttihinnoittelu tullut omassa taloudessa halvemmaksi vai kalliimmaksi.

”Sähkön hinta saattaa moninkertaistua hetkessä. Virtasen avulla voi laskea helposti, minkälainen sähkösopimus olisi tällä hetkellä oman kulutuksen kohdalla kaikkein järkevin”, palvelun kehittämisestä vastannut Nitorin data-asiantuntija Esa Puttonen kertoo.

title: Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education
content:
“Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”

title: Switzerland is Prosecuting the First Journalist Under its Banking Secrecy Law. The EU Has No Comment.
content:
The unprecedented criminal prosecution of a journalist under Switzerland's stringent banking secrecy law is raising alarms among press freedom advocates across Europe. But the European Union has nothing to say about it.

Lukas Hässig, founder of the financial news website Inside Paradeplatz, was charged in October over articles published a decade ago. The articles cited leaked information, and focused on financial dealings involving former Raiffeisen Switzerland chief executive Pierin Vincenz, and his business partner Beat Stocker.

The revelations helped trigger investigations that eventually led to criminal proceedings. In April 2022, Vincenz and Stocker were convicted of fraud and other offenses. Vincenz was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison, while Stocker received a four-year term. Both have appealed, with a ruling expected in January 2027.

Separately, Stocker filed a criminal complaint asking prosecutors to pursue charges against Hässig.

"There is a public interest in the facts. An unsubstantiated, flawed narrative is another matter," Stocker told OCCRP, arguing that there was “no legal basis under Swiss criminal law” for his own conviction.

title: How Leo Tolstoy Became a Vegetarian and Jumpstarted the Vegetarian & Humanitarian Movements in the 19th Century
content:
Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker, “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

title: EU sanctions Russian trolls, hackers
content:
European Union member countries on Monday issued sanctions against a Russian company running disinformation campaigns and one of Russia’s most well-known hacking groups.

The Council of the EU said it had sanctioned the Social Design Agency, a Moscow-based firm that carries out “large scale information manipulation and interference projects,” as well as 24 of its staff members.

The Social Design Agency is “funded, directed and supervised” by the Russian government and has organized disinformation campaigns targeting EU countries, EU institutions and European support for Ukraine, Council said.

The group has been connected in the past to a vast online disinformation network known as Doppelganger. It targeted the 2024 European elections and carried out “dedicated operations against EU member states such as Germany and France,” countries said.

EU capitals also agreed to levy sanctions against notorious Russian hacking group NoName057(16), which has targeted government bodies and critical infrastructure as well as private firms in the EU, Ukraine and the United States.

title: Kenen ehdoilla Suomea rakennetaan?
content:
Tekoäly muuttaa maailmaa nopeammin kuin ehdimme sitä ymmärtää. Puhutaan murroksesta, jota verrataan teolliseen vallankumoukseen. Se vaikuttaa siihen, millaista työtä teemme, miten turvallisuudestamme huolehditaan ja kenellä on valtaa. Tämä murros ei tapahdu vain jossain pilvessä. Sen fyysinen muoto on datakeskus: valtava halli, joka tarvitsee maata, sähköä, kriittisiä raaka-aineita ja usein vettä.

Juuri nyt maailmalla on käynnissä datakeskusbuumi, ja Suomi kiinnostaa. Meillä on vakaa yhteiskunta, toimiva sähköverkko, viileä ilmasto ja puhdasta, edullista energiaa. Siksi kansainväliset jättiyhtiöt katsovat tänne.

Se ei ole ongelma sinänsä, mutta ongelma on siinä, kenen ehdoilla jättiyhtiöiden datakeskuksia nousee Suomeen – kenen ehdoilla Suomea rakennetaan. Datakeskukset voivat tuoda Suomeen työtä, osaamista ja verotuloja, mutta jos annamme niiden tulla millä ehdoilla tahansa, havahdumme liian myöhään seurauksiin. Silloin metsät, vedet ja yhteinen sähkömme muuttuvat raaka-aineeksi, josta hyöty valuu muualle ja haitat jäävät tänne. Siksi meillä vihreillä on selkeä kanta: Suomi ei voi olla datakeskusten villi länsi.

title: Putin’s Propagandists Promise the Peace of the Graveyard
content:
The outcome of the midterm elections in the United States filled the studios of the Russian state media outlets with unadulterated sorrow.   

During his radio show Full Contact on November 4, state TV host Vladimir Solovyov grimly surmised, “Trumpushka failed.” Appearing on the state TV program Sunday Evening With Vladimir Solovyov last week, the head of RT Margarita Simonyan dramatically exclaimed that US President Donald Trump was America’s last hope.  

In reality, it seems to be the Kremlin’s last hope of achieving Ukraine’s unconditional capitulation by severing US support. The US still sells weapons to Ukraine and provides intelligence, although military and financial aid was largely terminated in early 2025, and Starlink satellite services continue to be limited, 

But Moscow wants much more. Pundits and experts explicitly say that they aim to reach and influence the American president, believing their words on state media are conveyed to Trump by the US Embassy in Russia.

title: Is this really the future we want?
content: Nine robots dance clumsily on the stage of Lisbon's FIL Arena. “This is our time, this is our fight” go the lyrics of the song. “This was the biggest robot dance performance outside of China!” the event's moderator proclaims. The 30,000 people in the arena give the robots a round of applause. The cameras filming the robots, however, are still operated by human videographers. I'm at the opening of Web Summit, one of the world's largest tech conferences, held annually in Lisbon. It draws 70,000 attendees encompassing the entire tech sector, from mega-corporations such as Meta, Apple, and Tiktok, to small start-ups, as well as countries from around the world showing off their industry. Attendees pay a lot to be there. General admission tickets cost around €1,500, unless you're a journalist, then you get in for free. I went to find out what the tech sector envisions for the future. Its biggest buzzword right now is agentic AI, which is marketed as a personal assistant for your daily life: think booking flights, working with Excel spreadsheets, or replying to that email you've left sitting in your inbox for too long. But that's not all. Listen to the AI companies and you'd think agentic

title: Cycling Connects: Bringing Tourism and Transport Together for a More Connected Baltic Sea Region
content:
Almost 80 participants joined the “Cycling Connects” webinar on 26 October 2026, marking the first jointly organised thematic event by the EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region (EUSBSR) Policy Areas Tourism and Transport. The strong interest and lively exchange confirmed that cycling tourism is much more than a tourism product – it is an important link between sustainable mobility, regional development and cross-border cooperation.

The webinar brought together representatives of the European Commission, European cycling organisations, regional authorities, tourism stakeholders and EU-funded projects to exchange perspectives, showcase practical initiatives and explore how closer cooperation between tourism and transport can support a more sustainable and accessible Baltic Sea Region.

Cycling tourism is growing in importance across Europe, offering opportunities to encourage low-carbon travel, connect urban and rural destinations, support local businesses and develop attractive cross-border tourism experiences. Yet unlocking its full potential requires cooperation across sectors, administrative borders and policy areas.

title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
content:
Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess. 

The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble. 

The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund. 

Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.

content:
Helsingin Suvilahdessa 29.–30.5.2027 järjestettävä Maailma kylässä -festivaali on avannut näytteilleasettajien paikkahaun sekä avoimen taiteilijahaun, jolla etsitään osallistavaa taideteosta, -tekoa tai -tempausta festivaalille. Järjestöille suunnattu puheohjelmahaku on avoinna 1.12. asti.

Jaa

Suomen suurimmalla kestävän kehityksen festarilla organisaatiot voivat kohdata uusia yleisöjä, tehdä toimintaansa tunnetuksi ja edistää itselleen tärkeitä tavoitteita. Mukaan voi tulla näytteilleasettajana, ruoka- tai käsityömyyjänä, kumppanina, ohjelmatuottajana tai mainostajana. Festareilla on paikkoja myös liikkuville myyntikärryille, feissaajille ja räätälöidyille erikoistoteutuksille.

Festivaalin näytteilleasettajapaikkojen haku on nyt avattu. Verkkosivuiltamme löytyy monenlaista tietoa osallistumisen suunnittelun tueksi: muun muassa alustava aluekartta, hinnasto, osallistumisehdot sekä tietoa erilaisista paikkavaihtoehdoista. Ruokamyyjille on erikseen kootut osallistumisohjeet.

Voit myös kysyä tarkempaa tietoa festivaalitiimiltä, joka auttaa mielellään löytämään juuri teille sopivan tavan tulla mukaan festivaalille.

title: People's Climate March: Thousands Demonstrate in Turkey as Country Hosts COP31 U.N. Summit
content:
Democracy Now! is in Antalya, Turkey, where this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, is being held. For the second year in a row, the United States has not sent an official delegation to the international talks, in keeping with the Trump administration’s longstanding hostility to such efforts to address the climate crisis.

There are nearly 100,000 participants here at this year’s climate summit, including many civil society activists from Turkey and around the globe. Over the weekend, Democracy Now! was in the streets of Antalya to speak with some of the thousands of protesters who marched to demand urgent climate action, including many labor leaders.

“Trade unions care about a lot more than just protecting jobs. We have systemic demands,” said Lala Peñaranda, the Latin America coordinator for Trade Unions for Energy Democracy.

title: Monique Wittigin feminismin klassikkoteos kyseenalaistaa itsestäänselvyyksinä pidettyjä käsityksiä sukupuolesta, kielestä ja kirjallisuudesta
content:
Kirjailija, sukupuolentutkija, kirjallisuudentutkija ja feministi Monique Wittigin (1935–2003) esseekokoelma Straight-ajattelu (The Straight Mind and Other Essays, 1992) käsittelee edelleen ajankohtaisia sekä vähälle huomiolle nykykeskustelussa jääneitä teemoja. Hänen mukaansa sukupuoli pohjaa oletukseen ”miehen” ja ”naisen” luonnollisuudesta, mutta tähän poliittiseen straight-ajatteluun voidaan puuttua kieltä muokkaamalla ja kirjallisuuden avulla. Teoksen on suomentanut Heta Rundgren.

”Sorto luo sukupuolen, ei toisinpäin.”

Ranskalaisen toisen aallon kuuluisimpiin feministeihin lukeutuva Monique Wittig toimi paitsi Ranskassa myös Yhdysvalloissa ja kirjoitti sekä ranskaksi että englanniksi. Hänen teoreettinen työnsä on vaikuttanut vahvasti esimerkiksi queer-ajatteluun.

”Hän kehitti sukupuolen ja seksuaalisuuden kriittistä tutkimusta mutta myös ajattelua kielen ja sukupuolen yhteyksistä. Hänen elämäntyönsä inspiroi laajasti nykypäivän feminististä ajattelua ja tutkimusta ympäri maailman”, suomentaja Heta Rundgren kertoo.

content:

title: Philippines: US Tech Hub to Displace Hundreds
content:
(Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch said today.

The Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities. The framework agreement between the Philippines and the United States is yet to be signed.

“Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should follow domestic laws and international standards that protect land rights.”

Human Rights Watch visited two affected sites in Capas in October 2026—Sapang Kawayan in Barangay Aranguren and Sitio Binyayan in Barangay O’Donnell—and spoke to 11 residents.

title: Estonia has a plan for Russian occupation: Run its government from the cloud
content:
TALLINN — Imagine French General Charles de Gaulle, exiled in London during World War II, running his Free France government by logging into the cloud.

Officials in Estonia are preparing for exactly such a scenario with a new strategy to boost doomsday resilience — hukukindlus in Estonian — that would allow the government’s digital services to be run entirely from abroad if its territory is occupied by a foreign enemy.

The Baltic country of  1.3 million, which shares a 294-kilometer border with Russia, fears it is a prime target if Moscow were to invade a European Union country. Security services have already warned that Russia is waging a hybrid war on Europe, and Estonia has blamed Moscow for everything from cyberattacks to arson plots to cuts to undersea data cables.

Now, Tallinn is preparing to move its public services to the cloud “either when data centers are destroyed or there’s boots on the ground and we cannot operate,” said Tõnu Grünberg, an architect of the new strategy and former deputy secretary general for digital infrastructure and cybersecurity at Estonia’s Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs.

title: Vain joka viides 9.-luokkalainen opiskelee kolmea kieltä
content:
Tilastokeskus on julkaissut tilastoja perusopetuksen ainevalinnoista vuonna 2025. Kieltenopetus kapenee ja yksipuolistuu edelleen: 91 prosenttia vuosiluokkien 7–9 oppilaista opiskeli ensimmäisenä pitkänä vieraana kielenä eli A1-kielenä englantia. A1-saksaa opiskeli 0,9 % oppilaista, A1-ranskaa ja A1-ruotsia kumpaakin 0,8 %. Valinnaista kolmatta kieltä opiskeli seitsemännellä luokalla 12 %, kahdeksannella luokalla 19 % ja yhdeksännellä luokalla 20 % oppilaista.

Luvut kertovat toteutuneesta kieltenopetuksesta – eivät siitä, kuinka moni peruskoululainen olisi halunnut kieliä opiskella. Koulujen rakenteet kuten ryhmäkokovaatimukset ja lukujärjestystekniset asiat vaikuttavat voimakkaasti kielten ryhmien syntymiseen.

title: Ecuadorian Courts Expose Flaws in US High-Seas Arrests
content:
Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats. They detained 146 of the 160 crew members and transferred them to Ecuadorian authorities, who charged 90 with “unlawful association.”

Since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people. In an October 29 judgment reviewed by Human Rights Watch, a Manta judge acquitted eight fishermen from a vessel named the Don Rufo. The prosecution’s own witnesses, including Ecuadorian police and Navy officials, testified that no illicit items were recovered, and that they knew of no prior investigation linking the fishermen to organized crime.

The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.

title: UAE: 5 Shia Residents Arrested Arbitrarily
content:
(Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity. 

Emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said. 

“Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” said Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.”

Between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the company that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives.

title: Hanoi 2015: The City Conceded on Trees, Not on Accountability
content:
The Tree Hugs movement won the argument over trees and lost the argument over accountability. Its petition to Hanoi’s People’s Committee made three demands: stop the felling, open up the decision, and hold officials to account. The first was met within four days. The other two never were. That gap is the lesson.

The movement began with a dismissal. On 17 March 2015, a Hanoi propaganda official was asked whether residents had been consulted about plans to fell 6,700 street trees. There was no need, he replied. Within days, tens of thousands of Hanoians had answered him on Facebook.

No single organisation led the response. It was a loose network of three Facebook groups, drawing mostly young people and women.

No single organisation led the response. It was a loose network of three Facebook groups, drawing mostly young people and women.

The plan was approved in late 2013 without public notice. It would replace 6,708 trees on 190 streets for about US$3.4 million. Officials called it landscaping. Residents saw healthy, century old trees, many planted under French rule, falling within days in a city that shelters under their shade.

title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
content:
Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.
snippet: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
content:
On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital.

Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.

The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital. 

When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container.

“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.

title: Kazakhstan and Japan Renew Test-Ban Appeal as Treaty Deadlock Persists
content:
Thirty years after opening for signature, the CTBT has broad international support but still lacks nine ratifications required for entry into force

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | 15 November 2026 (IDN) — Kazakhstan and Japan have renewed calls for an end to nuclear testing as the treaty intended to prohibit all nuclear explosions remains blocked, three decades after it opened for signature.

Their appeal, made at a September commemoration at the United Nations Office at Nairobi, comes as preparations for enforcing the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) continue despite the political impasse. An inspection exercise in Namibia is testing capabilities that cannot be used under the treaty until it enters into force.

The contrast exposes a central weakness in the international effort to prevent renewed testing: governments have built a global detection network, but have yet to activate the agreement that would authorise inspectors to investigate a suspected violation on the ground.

title: Petition for the Creation of the European Public Social Network
content:
Social media in their current form are great for Big Tech companies making money selling our attention and training their machine learning models on our data using unsustainable, energy-heavy computations. Their business model turns out to be fertile ground for disinformation, conspiracies, affective polarization, and further marginalization of certain voices. Deep down, we all want to leave but we stay because we fear losing the means of communication with others. But where individual resistance seems futile, collective action could be the solution.

The good news is, there is a plenty of talent in the EU already, making alternatives not just easy to imagine, but ready to be observed. We strive to gather public support for the creation of a decentralized social network for everyone, where users have full control over their private data and the algorithm and where bots and fake accounts spreading disinformation are prevented from accessing the platform. As students from across the EU joined by other citizens, we ask the European Commission to support the creation of a European public-service social network financed and controlled by citizens.

This interview is part of the African Languages Digital Activism series by Rising Voices, highlighting the personal journeys of activists working to preserve, promote, and revitalise African languages. Through their stories, the series explores the role of digital platforms, community initiatives, and local knowledge in strengthening the presence of African languages both online and offline.

title: Mass protests that led to regime change had their heyday between 1980 and 2011: what happened?
content:
People are taking to the streets across the world. In 2025, mass mobilisation occurred in countries such as Morocco, Tanzania and Turkey. In Madagascar, protests resulted in president Andry Rajoelina fleeing the country in October. More recently, protesters have filled the streets from France and Italy to Senegal and Kenya.

By mass mobilisation, we mean sustained, organised campaigns of protests that involve more than 1,000 people, aimed at changing a country’s political regime or removing the government or leader.

Mass mobilisation has historically been seen as a viable path to democracy. Ferdinand Marcos left Manila in 1986 after weeks of popular protests. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 after months of demonstrations in East Germany. South Africa’s apartheid regime yielded to domestic and international pressure in the 1990s.

The examples are many, and mass movements have been a driving force to democratic change in authoritarian regimes.

title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
content:
Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks

The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.

title: The EU has always found a way through. On AI, it’s struggling to see it.
content:
There might be an AI apocalypse. European leaders don’t really want to talk about it.

By SEBASTIAN STARCEVIC and PIETER HAECK
in DUBLIN

Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

The European Union wasn’t set up to deal with challenges as vast and existential as the possibility of AI wiping out humanity.

For two decades, the EU’s leaders have muddled through crisis after crisis — from Greece coming within days of being pushed out of the eurozone, to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which forced millions to seek safety in the bloc. Each time, it has found a way through. It’s what the EU does.

With AI, though, it’s turning out to be different.

Tech experts, industry and even governments themselves describe paralysis, distraction and defeatism in Europe’s capitals. It’s telling that it took four years after the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 for EU leaders to bring themselves to discuss artificial intelligence at a summit in Dublin on Friday.

And even then, there was little enthusiasm for the topic.

title: After School MeToo: Political Mamas’ Fight for Answers in South Korea
content:
During South Korea’s 2018 School MeToo movement, students publicly reported sexual harassment and assault by teachers. But another question remained: how had schools and education authorities responded?

In 2019, Political Mamas, a South Korean nonprofit founded by mothers, and open to other caregivers, began requesting records from regional education offices and mapping publicly reported allegations.

The campaign aimed to make institutional responses visible, identify gaps in investigations and disciplinary action, and strengthen accountability for student safety.

South Korea’s wider #MeToo movement gained momentum in early 2018 after prosecutor Seo Ji-hyun publicly described sexual harassment she had experienced. One Yonghwa graduate later told WomenNews that seeing Seo and Hollywood actresses speak out had encouraged her to do the same.

title: ‘Risk multiplier’: super El Niño looms over Cop31 as climate pattern fuels global disasters
content:
Strongest El Niño in centuries adds urgency to UN climate talks as vulnerable countries face ‘compounding’ crises

If the galloping pace of the climate crisis isn’t enough to spur countries to act at UN climate talks under way in Turkey, there is another major threat heightening its havoc: the strongest El Niño event in at least 1,000 years.

The “jaw-dropping” El Niño, a naturally recurring phenomenon where the eastern Pacific heats up every few years with temporary but global implications, has provided added urgency to wrangling at the Cop31 summit over climate funding for vulnerable countries that are having to scramble to respond.

title: Small Steps 4 Hannah: How One Family Helped Queensland See Coercive Control
content:
In February 2020, Hannah Clarke and her three children, Aaliyah, Laianah and Trey, were murdered in Brisbane, Queensland, Australia, by the husband she had recently left. Her father, Lloyd Clarke, kept asking how he had missed the signs.

Part of the answer was a term many people did not know yet: coercive control. It means using a pattern of behaviour to dominate a partner, such as cutting her off from family, tracking her, and controlling her money. This abuse often leaves no visible injuries.

Within weeks, Hannah’s parents, Sue and Lloyd Clarke, set up the Small Steps 4 Hannah Foundation. It supports people affected by domestic violence, teaches students, workers and families to spot coercive control, and has pushed the Queensland Government to make it a crime.

This article argues that Small Steps used one family’s story to make hidden abuse visible and help write it into law in 2024. Whether the law brings real safety is still unclear.

In its 2016–17 Annual Report, Queensland’s Domestic and Family Violence Death Review and Advisory Board found signs of coercive control in almost all the deaths it reviewed. Yet services rarely responded unless physical violence was also reported.

Lana Nusseibeh appears to have the support of Russia and the US, but her role glossing the horror in Sudan makes her unsuitable – and we should say so

Since the devastating war in Sudan began in 2023, some of the best investigative work uncovering those responsible has been carried out by the UN panel of experts. Its reports have revealed clear evidence that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been funnelling weapons and providing mercenaries to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide.

It is these reports, produced by UN-funded investigators, that the UN secretary general, António Guterres, cites whenever he speaks about Sudan.
